title: Mistress Mary Quite Contrary
paragraphs: Mary had liked to watch her mother from far away, and she had thought her very pretty. But she hardly knew her, so no one could have expected her to love her, or to miss her much now that she was gone. In fact, she did not miss her at all. Mary was a child who thought only of herself, and she went on thinking only of herself, as she always had. If she had been older, she would surely have been frightened to find herself alone in the world. But she was very young, and since people had always looked after her, she assumed they always would. What she really wondered was whether she was going to live with nice people, who would be polite to her and let her have her own way, as her Ayah and the other native servants had done.

She knew she would not be staying at the English clergyman’s house, where she had been taken at first. She did not want to stay there anyway. The clergyman was poor, and he had five children, all nearly the same age. They wore shabby clothes, and they were always quarreling and snatching toys from one another. Mary hated their messy little bungalow, and she was so unpleasant to the children that after a day or two nobody would play with her. By the second day they had given her a nickname, and it made her furious.

Basil was the one who thought of it first. He was a small boy with cheeky blue eyes and a turned-up nose, and Mary hated him. She was playing by herself under a tree, just as she had been playing on the day the cholera broke out. She was piling up heaps of earth and making paths for a garden, and Basil came and stood close by to watch her. After a while he grew rather interested, and all at once he had an idea to offer.
“Why don’t you put a heap of stones there and pretend it’s a rockery?” he said. “There, in the middle.” And he leaned over her to point.
“Go away!” cried Mary. “I don’t want boys around. Go away!”
For a moment Basil looked angry, and then he started to tease her. He was always teasing his sisters. He danced around and around her, making faces, singing and laughing.

“Mistress Mary, quite contrary,
How does your garden grow?
With silver bells, and cockle shells,
And marigolds all in a row.”

He kept singing it until the other children heard him and laughed too. The angrier Mary got, the more they sang “Mistress Mary, quite contrary.” After that, for as long as she stayed with them, they called her “Mistress Mary Quite Contrary” whenever they talked about her to each other, and often when they talked to her.
“You’re going to be sent home,” Basil told her, “at the end of the week. And we’re glad of it.”
“I’m glad of it too,” Mary answered. “Where is home?”

“She doesn’t even know where home is!” said Basil, with all the scorn of a seven-year-old. “It’s England, of course. Our grandmama lives there, and our sister Mabel was sent to her last year. But you’re not going to your grandmama. You don’t have one. You’re going to your uncle. His name is Mr. Archibald Craven.”
“I don’t know anything about him,” Mary snapped.

“I know you don’t,” Basil answered. “You don’t know anything. Girls never do. I heard Father and Mother talking about him. He lives in a huge, lonely old house in the country, and nobody goes near him. He’s so cross that he won’t let them, and they wouldn’t come even if he did. He’s a hunchback, and he’s horrible.”
“I don’t believe you,” said Mary. She turned her back and stuck her fingers in her ears, because she would not listen to another word.

But she thought about it a great deal afterward. That night Mrs. Crawford told her she would be sailing to England in a few days to live with her uncle, Mr. Archibald Craven, at Misselthwaite Manor. Mary looked so stony and stubbornly uninterested that they did not know what to make of her. They tried to be kind to her, but she simply turned her face away when Mrs. Crawford tried to kiss her, and she held herself stiff when Mr. Crawford patted her shoulder.

“She’s such a plain child,” Mrs. Crawford said afterward, with pity in her voice. “And her mother was such a pretty creature, with such a pretty manner too. Mary has the most unattractive ways I have ever seen in a child. The children call her ‘Mistress Mary Quite Contrary,’ and though it’s naughty of them, you can’t help understanding why.”

“Perhaps if her mother had brought her pretty face and her pretty manners into the nursery more often, Mary might have learned some pretty ways too. It’s very sad, now that the poor beautiful woman is gone, to think that many people never even knew she had a child at all.”

“I believe she hardly ever looked at her,” sighed Mrs. Crawford. “When her Ayah died, there was nobody left to spare a thought for the poor little thing. Imagine the servants running away and leaving her all alone in that empty bungalow. Colonel McGrew said he nearly jumped out of his skin when he opened the door and found her standing by herself in the middle of the room.”

Mary made the long voyage to England in the care of an officer’s wife, who was taking her own children to leave them at a boarding school. The woman was wrapped up in her own little boy and girl, and she was rather glad to hand Mary over to the woman Mr. Archibald Craven had sent to meet her in London. That woman was his housekeeper at Misselthwaite Manor, and her name was Mrs. Medlock. She was a stout woman with very red cheeks and sharp black eyes. She wore a very purple dress, a black silk cape trimmed with shiny black beads, and a black bonnet with purple velvet flowers that stuck up and trembled whenever she moved her head. Mary did not like her at all. But Mary seldom liked anyone, so that was nothing unusual, and it was plain enough that Mrs. Medlock did not think much of her either.
“My word! She’s a plain little thing, isn’t she?” she said. “And we’d heard her mother was a beauty. She hasn’t passed much of it down, has she, ma’am?”
“Perhaps she’ll improve as she grows older,” the officer’s wife said kindly. “If she weren’t so sallow, and had a nicer expression, her features are really quite good. Children change so much.”
“She’ll have to change a good deal,” answered Mrs. Medlock. “And there’s nothing at Misselthwaite likely to improve children—if you ask me!”

They thought Mary was not listening, because she was standing a little apart from them at the window of the private hotel where they had gone. She was watching the buses and cabs and people go by, but she heard every word, and it made her very curious about her uncle and the place where he lived. What sort of place was it, and what would he be like? What was a hunchback? She had never seen one. Perhaps there were none in India.

Ever since she had been living in other people’s houses, with no Ayah, she had begun to feel lonely and to have strange thoughts that were new to her. She had begun to wonder why she had never seemed to belong to anyone, even when her father and mother were alive. Other children seemed to belong to their fathers and mothers, but she had never really seemed to be anyone’s little girl. She had had servants, and food, and clothes, but nobody had paid any attention to her. She did not know this was because she was a disagreeable child. Of course, she did not know she was disagreeable. She often thought other people were, but she had no idea that she was too.

She thought Mrs. Medlock was the most disagreeable person she had ever seen, with her common, brightly colored face and her common, fancy bonnet. The next day they set out on their journey to Yorkshire. Mary walked through the station to the train carriage with her head held high, trying to stay as far away from Mrs. Medlock as she could, because she did not want to seem to belong to her. It would have made her angry to think that people took her for Mrs. Medlock’s little girl.

But Mrs. Medlock was not in the least bothered by Mary or her thoughts. She was the kind of woman who would “stand no nonsense from young ones.” At least, that is what she would have said if anyone had asked her. She had not wanted to go to London just when her sister Maria’s daughter was about to be married. But she had a comfortable, well-paid job as housekeeper at Misselthwaite Manor, and the only way to keep it was to do at once whatever Mr. Archibald Craven told her to do. She never dared even to ask a question.

“Captain Lennox and his wife died of the cholera,” Mr. Craven had told her in his short, cold way. “Captain Lennox was my wife’s brother, and I am their daughter’s guardian. The child is to be brought here. You must go to London and bring her yourself.”
So she packed her small trunk and made the journey.

Mary sat in her corner of the railway carriage, looking plain and fretful. She had nothing to read and nothing to look at, so she folded her thin little black-gloved hands in her lap. Her black dress made her look more yellow than ever, and her limp, light hair straggled out from under her black crêpe hat.

“I never saw a more marred-looking young one in my whole life,” Mrs. Medlock thought. (Marred is a Yorkshire word, and it means spoiled and pettish.) She had never seen a child who could sit so still and do nothing. At last she got tired of watching her and began to talk in a brisk, hard voice.
“I suppose I may as well tell you something about where you’re going,” she said. “Do you know anything about your uncle?”
“No,” said Mary.
“You never heard your father and mother talk about him?”
“No,” said Mary, frowning. She frowned because she remembered that her father and mother had never talked to her about anything in particular. They had certainly never told her things.
“Humph,” muttered Mrs. Medlock, staring at her odd, unresponsive little face. She said nothing more for a few moments, and then she began again.
“I suppose you might as well be told something, to get you ready. You’re going to a strange place.”
Mary said nothing at all. Mrs. Medlock seemed rather put out by her obvious lack of interest, but after taking a breath she went on.

“Not that it isn’t a grand big place in a gloomy way, and Mr. Craven is proud of it in his way—and that’s gloomy enough too. The house is six hundred years old, and it stands on the edge of the moor. There are nearly a hundred rooms in it, though most of them are shut up and locked. And there are paintings and fine old furniture and things that have been there for ages, and a big park around it, with gardens and trees whose branches trail to the ground—some of them do.” She paused and took another breath. “But there’s nothing else,” she finished suddenly.

Mary had begun to listen in spite of herself. It all sounded so unlike India, and anything new rather appealed to her. But she did not mean to look interested. That was one of her unhappy, disagreeable ways. So she sat still.
“Well,” said Mrs. Medlock. “What do you think of it?”
“Nothing,” she answered. “I don’t know anything about such places.”
That made Mrs. Medlock give a short laugh.
“Eh!” she said. “But you talk like an old woman. Don’t you care?”
“It doesn’t matter,” said Mary, “whether I care or not.”

“You’re right about that,” said Mrs. Medlock. “It doesn’t. I don’t know why you’re to be kept at Misselthwaite Manor, unless it’s because that’s the easiest way. _He’s_ not going to trouble himself about you, that’s certain. He never troubles himself about anyone.”
She stopped herself, as if she had just remembered something in time.
“He has a crooked back,” she said. “That’s what soured him. He was a sour young man and got no good out of all his money and his big house until he was married.”

Mary’s eyes turned toward her, in spite of her plan not to seem to care. She had never thought of a hunchback being married, and she was a little surprised. Mrs. Medlock saw this, and since she was a talkative woman, she went on with more interest. At any rate, it was one way of passing the time.

“She was a sweet, pretty thing, and he’d have walked the whole world over to get her a blade of grass she wanted. Nobody thought she’d marry him, but she did, and people said she married him for his money. But she didn’t—she didn’t,” she said firmly. “When she died—”
Mary gave a little jump, without meaning to.

“Oh! She died?” she exclaimed, quite without meaning to. She had just remembered a French fairy story she had once read, called “Riquet à la Houppe.” It was about a poor hunchback and a beautiful princess, and it suddenly made her feel sorry for Mr. Archibald Craven.

“Yes, she died,” Mrs. Medlock answered. “And it made him stranger than ever. He cares about nobody. He won’t see people. Most of the time he goes away, and when he is at Misselthwaite he shuts himself up in the West Wing and won’t let anyone see him but Pitcher. Pitcher is an old fellow, but he took care of Mr. Craven when he was a child, and he knows his ways.”

It sounded like something from a book, and it did not make Mary feel cheerful. A house with a hundred rooms, nearly all of them shut up with their doors locked—a house on the edge of a moor, whatever a moor was—sounded dreary. And a man with a crooked back who shut himself up too! She stared out of the window with her lips pressed tightly together. It seemed only natural that the rain should have begun to pour down in gray slanting lines, splashing and streaming down the window panes. If the pretty wife had been alive, she might have made things cheerful. She might have been something like Mary’s own mother, running in and out and going to parties, as her mother had done, in dresses “full of lace.” But she was not there any more.

“You needn’t expect to see him, because ten to one you won’t,” said Mrs. Medlock. “And you mustn’t expect people to talk to you. You’ll have to play about and look after yourself. You’ll be told which rooms you can go into and which you’re to keep out of. There are gardens enough. But when you’re in the house, don’t go wandering and poking about. Mr. Craven won’t have it.”

“I won’t want to go poking about,” said sour little Mary. And just as suddenly as she had begun to feel a little sorry for Mr. Archibald Craven, she stopped feeling sorry and decided he was unpleasant enough to deserve everything that had happened to him.

She turned her face toward the streaming panes of the carriage window and gazed out at the gray rainstorm, which looked as if it would go on forever and ever. She watched it so long and so steadily that the grayness grew heavier and heavier before her eyes, and she fell asleep.
